title: GOD WARNED THE KINGS OF ISRAEL NOT TO MULTIPLY WIVES. SOLOMON HAD 1,000 WOMEN IN HIS LIFE—AND STILL LOST THE ONE THING HE COULD NOT AFFORD TO LOSE.
paragraphs: GOD WARNED THE KINGS OF ISRAEL NOT TO MULTIPLY WIVES. SOLOMON HAD 1,000 WOMEN IN HIS LIFE—AND STILL LOST THE ONE THING HE COULD NOT AFFORD TO LOSE.

He had wisdom beyond ordinary men, wealth beyond imagination, and a kingdom that nations admired. But the most dangerous thing Solomon accumulated was not gold, horses, or power. It was the very thing God had warned him would turn his heart away. And what happened to Solomon may expose something we have been refusing to confront in our own lives.
There is something terrifying about the story of Solomon.
Not because he was a wicked man who never knew God.
But because he was a man who knew God, received extraordinary wisdom from God, experienced the blessings of God, built a magnificent temple for the worship of God…
And still allowed his heart to wander.
Read that again.
A man can know the Scriptures, speak beautifully about God, accomplish extraordinary things in God's name, and still be quietly surrendering the very heart God desires.
Solomon did not begin his reign as a man bowing before foreign gods.
He began as a young king who knew he needed divine wisdom.
But somewhere between the prayer that made him famous and the compromises that destroyed his faithfulness, something changed.
And the frightening part?
The change did not happen overnight.
It happened one decision at a time.
One exception.
One rationalization.
One desire he refused to surrender.
Until the man who once asked God for wisdom became the man whose life demonstrated why wisdom without obedience is never enough.
But before we judge Solomon, we need to hear the warning God gave centuries before Solomon ever sat on Israel's throne.
Because this warning was not merely about ancient royal marriages.
It was about the human heart.
And it is still speaking to ours.
In Deuteronomy 17:17, God gave this command concerning Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.” — Deuteronomy 17:17, KJV
Notice something.
God did not simply prohibit multiplying wives.
He explained why.
“That his heart turn not away.”
In the Hebrew text, the warning includes these words:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo.
A close translation is:
“And he shall not multiply wives for himself, so that his heart does not turn aside.”
The Hebrew word לְבָבוֹ (levavo) means “his heart.”
But in biblical Hebrew, the heart is far more than the seat of romantic feelings.
It is the inner person—the center of thought, desire, intention, and moral commitment.
And the verb יָסוּר (yasur), from the Hebrew root sur, expresses the idea of turning aside or departing.
God was warning Israel's kings against accumulating wives in a way that would turn their inner allegiance away from Him.
This was not an arbitrary restriction from a God who wanted to deny kings happiness.
It was a protective command from the God who knew exactly what unchecked royal appetite could do.
And there is something else we must understand.
The warning appears alongside commands against multiplying horses and accumulating excessive silver and gold (Deuteronomy 17:16–17).
These were symbols of royal military strength, wealth, prestige, and political security.
In the ancient world, royal marriages could also establish alliances between kingdoms.
A king could begin trusting his army, his treasury, his political connections, and his marriages more than the Lord who had placed him on the throne.
God was not merely addressing the number of women in a palace.
He was confronting the temptation to build a kingdom on everything except dependence upon Him.
A king was supposed to lead God's people under God's authority.
He was never supposed to become so powerful that he imagined himself above God's Word.
And this is where Solomon's story becomes painfully personal.
Because we may not possess a royal palace.
We may not command armies.
We may not have seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.
But we understand what it means to want something so badly that we begin negotiating with what God has already said.
We understand the dangerous whisper:
“Just this once.”
“God knows my heart.”
“It's not hurting anybody.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“I'm still serving God.”
And perhaps the most dangerous one of all:
“I'm strong enough to handle this.”
Solomon may have thought he was strong enough too.
Scripture tells us that God appeared to Solomon and gave him wisdom and understanding beyond ordinary measure (1 Kings 3:5–12; 4:29–34).
People came from distant lands to hear him.
His kingdom prospered.
His reputation spread.
The queen of Sheba came to test his wisdom and was astonished by what she encountered (1 Kings 10:1–9).
But admiration from the world does not make a person immune to spiritual compromise.
And spiritual gifting does not cancel the need for spiritual obedience.
Then we arrive at one of the saddest passages in the Old Testament.
“But king Solomon loved many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites.” — 1 Kings 11:1, KJV
The phrase “strange women” in the KJV refers here to foreign women, not women who behaved strangely.
And we must be careful not to misunderstand the passage.
The Bible is not teaching that ethnicity itself makes someone spiritually dangerous.
Ruth was a Moabite woman who embraced the God of Israel and became part of the family line through which Jesus Christ came (Ruth 1:16; 4:13–22; Matthew 1:5).
The central issue in Solomon's story was not racial identity.
It was covenant faithfulness and the worship of other gods.
First Kings 11:2 explicitly explains the danger: these marriages involved peoples whose religious practices could turn Israel's heart toward other gods.
The same verse says Solomon “clave unto these in love.”
He held fast to them.
And then comes the devastating record.
“And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.” — 1 Kings 11:3, KJV
Seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
One thousand women connected to his royal household.
Yet the deepest tragedy was not the staggering number.
It was the sentence that followed.
“And his wives turned away his heart.”
There it is.
The very consequence God had warned about in Deuteronomy.
What God said could happen…
Happened.
And the next verse makes it even more heartbreaking.

“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.” — 1 Kings 11:4, KJV
When Solomon was old.
Think about that.
He had lived long enough to see God's faithfulness.
Long enough to witness answered prayers.
Long enough to build the temple.
Long enough to know that the Lord was worthy of his complete devotion.
And yet, in the later years of his life, his heart was divided.
The Hebrew text describes his heart as not being שָׁלֵם (shalem) with the LORD.
The word carries the sense of being whole, complete, or undivided.
This does not mean David, his father, had lived a sinless life. David's own failures were grievous.
It means Solomon's allegiance had become divided in a way that stood in stark contrast to the wholehearted devotion God required.
And here is the question that should trouble every one of us:
What if the greatest danger to your faith is not the suffering that makes you cry out to God, but the comfort that slowly teaches you to live without Him?
Some people abandon their convictions under pressure.
Others gradually abandon them in prosperity.
Not because God has stopped being faithful.
But because their hearts have become attached to gifts, pleasures, relationships, and ambitions that have taken the place of the Giver.
Solomon had so much.
Yet his abundance did not protect his heart.
And sometimes we do the same thing.
We ask God to bless a relationship, but refuse to ask whether that relationship is leading us toward Him.
We pray for financial success, but quietly allow money to become our security.
We ask God to open doors, but stop listening when He tells us not to walk through one.
We want the blessings of obedience without surrendering the desires that obedience would confront.
And then we wonder why prayer feels distant.
Why Scripture no longer pierces us.
Why worship becomes routine.
Why we can still speak the language of faith while secretly living in spiritual compromise.
Not every season of spiritual dryness is caused by personal sin. Even faithful believers experience suffering, grief, exhaustion, and seasons of unanswered questions.
But sometimes, when our conscience grows quiet, it is worth asking whether we have been ignoring something God has already made clear.
Because a heart does not have to reject God loudly to begin drifting away from Him.
Sometimes it simply becomes too occupied with something else.
And the enemy does not need to persuade you to stop believing in God if he can persuade you to stop obeying Him.
Solomon's downfall went beyond private desire.
First Kings 11:5–8 records that he followed foreign deities and built high places associated with their worship.
His compromise became public.
His divided heart influenced the religious life of the kingdom.
The man who had built a temple dedicated to the LORD also became associated with places of worship for false gods.
Imagine the sorrow of that contrast.
The same king who once prayed that the nations would know the LORD (1 Kings 8:41–43) later participated in the very idolatry that contradicted that prayer.
This is what sin can do when it is repeatedly defended rather than confessed.
It does not merely ask for a place in your life.
It gradually demands a place in your worship.
And whatever begins to receive the trust, loyalty, obedience, and devotion that belong to God has become a rival to Him.
For one person, it may be a secret relationship.
For another, an addiction.
For another, the need for approval.
For another, the hunger to be admired.
For another, money.
For another, bitterness they refuse to release.
For another, a hidden sin they have learned to excuse because nobody else knows.
And perhaps you are reading this while carrying something you have never admitted to anyone.
You still attend church.
You still share Bible verses.
You still tell people God is good.
And He is.
But privately, there is a battle between what you know God says and what you have become unwilling to surrender.
You are tired of the battle.
Tired of the guilt.
Tired of promising yourself that tomorrow will be different.
And perhaps you are afraid that if people knew what was happening inside your heart, they would never look at you the same way again.
Listen carefully.
The fact that you are struggling does not mean you are beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
But neither should grace become an excuse to keep embracing what is destroying you.
Jesus did not come to make sin comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
He came to forgive, cleanse, redeem, and transform.
And sometimes His mercy begins by exposing the very thing we have spent years trying to hide.
That is why the warning to Solomon matters so much.
God did not warn him because God hated him.
God warned him because God knew where disobedience would lead.
And the same Lord who warns us against sin also invites us to turn back to Him.
But we must not soften the consequences in Solomon's story.
First Kings 11:9 says the LORD was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away.
God announced that the kingdom would be torn from his dynasty, though the full division would come during his son's reign, with a portion preserved for David's sake (1 Kings 11:11–13).
This was not a harmless private mistake.
It was covenant unfaithfulness with national consequences.
And Scripture does not explicitly tell us that Solomon personally repented before his death.
Some readers understand Ecclesiastes as evidence of Solomon's later reflection and repentance, but the biblical narrative does not give us a clear account of such a return.
We should not invent a happy ending that Scripture does not record.
Instead, we should allow the warning to stand.
Because not every consequence disappears simply because we eventually recognize our mistake.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
Restoration is real.
But sin can leave wounds that require time, accountability, and the healing work of God.
And now comes the most beautiful contrast in this entire story.
Solomon was a son of David who possessed extraordinary wisdom.
But Solomon was not the ultimate Son of David.
He was a king who received a kingdom and allowed his heart to become divided.
Jesus Christ is the promised King whose obedience was perfect.
Solomon multiplied wealth, royal relationships, and worldly security.
Jesus entered our world in humility.
Solomon's heart turned toward false gods.
Jesus remained faithful to the Father even when obedience led Him to the cross.
Solomon's disobedience contributed to the division of a kingdom.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus brings sinners into reconciliation with God and gathers a people who belong to Him.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a collection of warnings about becoming better people.
It is the announcement that God has provided the Savior we could never become for ourselves.
Jesus said:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10, KJV
And the apostle Paul wrote:
“For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” — Romans 5:19, KJV
The obedience of Christ is the foundation of our hope.
Not our reputation.
Not our religious accomplishments.
Not the number of verses we can quote.
Not how many people admire our faith.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Able to save those who come to God through Him.
And when we repent and trust in Him, we are not merely trying to become improved versions of our old selves.
We are turning to the Savior who forgives sin and gives new life.
This is the heartbeat of our message:
Not because our past never happened.
Not because our choices have no consequences.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the Gospel declares that sin and shame do not have to be the final word over a person who comes to Christ.
Perhaps you have been like Solomon.
Not in wealth.
Not in power.
But in the slow accumulation of compromises.
You remember when your prayers were sincere.
When opening the Bible felt like meeting with the God you loved.
When you could not imagine knowingly walking away from His Word.
But somewhere along the road, something entered your life that you did not want to surrender.
And now you are wondering whether you can ever become spiritually whole again.
Hear the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
You do not need to impress Jesus with a performance of perfection.
You need to come to Him in repentance and faith.
Bring Him the divided heart.
Bring Him the secret compromise.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the habits you have struggled to break.
Bring Him the relationship you know is drawing you away from Him.
Bring Him the ambition that has become your master.
And ask Him to teach you to love Him above everything else.
Not merely to feel guilty for a moment.
But to surrender.
To turn.
To obey.
To walk in the light.
To seek the help of mature believers when the battle is too heavy to fight alone.
To replace secrecy with truth.
To stop calling dangerous compromises harmless.
Because repentance is not simply feeling terrible about what we have done.
It is a Godward turning of the heart that bears fruit in a changed life.
And even that transformation is sustained by the grace of God.
There is a prayer in Psalm 86:11 that speaks directly to the tragedy of Solomon's divided heart:
“Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name.”
Unite my heart.
What a prayer.
Not merely, “Lord, give me more blessings.”
Not merely, “Lord, make me successful.”
Not merely, “Lord, remove every difficulty.”
But:
“Lord, give me a heart that belongs wholly to You.”
A heart that does not worship You on Sunday and willingly bow to sin in secret.
A heart that does not praise You publicly while refusing Your correction privately.
A heart that treasures Your presence more than applause.
A heart that would rather lose an opportunity than lose its integrity.
A heart that remembers that nothing this world offers is worth abandoning the One who gave His life to save us.
And perhaps that is the prayer you need tonight.
Not a longer speech.
Not another religious performance.
Just an honest confession.

“Lord Jesus, I have allowed things into my heart that are pulling me away from You. I have excused what You have warned me against. I have tried to hold on to You while refusing to let go of what is harming my soul. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Teach me to obey You. Unite my heart to fear Your name. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy, Your truth, and Your transforming grace. Amen.”
If that prayer reflects what you are facing, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to disclose private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
There are people reading this who may recognize their own struggle in your words.
Your honesty may remind someone that they do not have to keep pretending.
Not to glorify the past.
But to glorify the mercy of the Savior who met you there.
Someone needs to know that coming back to Christ is possible.
Someone needs to hear that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the turning of a sinner toward the One who gives hope.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not merely to increase its reach.

But because someone in your family, someone from your church, an old friend, a struggling believer, or someone who has never understood the Gospel may be living through the very battle this Scripture exposes.
Do it with kindness, not as a public accusation.
Because we do not want people merely to feel moved by a story.
We want them to encounter the truth of God's Word and be drawn toward Jesus Christ.
New resources are being added almost daily.
These resources are intended to help believers go beyond a passing emotional moment and develop a deeper, more grounded, more faithful relationship with Christ.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that helps sustain and expand the work of sharing biblical teaching, Christian resources, encouragement, and discipleship with others.
Scripture teaches that generosity toward faithful Gospel ministry is a meaningful expression of Christian stewardship (Philippians 4:15–18; 2 Corinthians 9:6–8).
The Bible teaches believers to give willingly, not under pressure.
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Your prayers, your encouragement, your thoughtful comments, and your willingness to share biblical truth with others are deeply valued.
These items can serve as reminders of Scripture, conversation starters about faith, and practical resources for Christian living.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
A ministry cannot forgive your sins.
Jesus can.
Christ's finished work is the foundation of our reconciliation.
And no amount of public Christian activity can replace a heart that has truly surrendered to Him.
That is the lesson Solomon's life leaves before us.
You can possess extraordinary knowledge and still need humility.
You can receive remarkable blessings and still need boundaries.
You can be admired by thousands and still need repentance.
You can build something magnificent for God while neglecting your own obedience to Him.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one question.
Not about Solomon.
About you.
What am I allowing to occupy a place in my heart that belongs to Jesus Christ alone?
Do not rush past the answer.
If the Holy Spirit is bringing a specific compromise to your attention through Scripture, do not bury that conviction beneath another distraction.
Bring it to the Lord.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Trust His grace.
And take the next faithful step.
Because the King who warned Solomon about a divided heart is the same God who, through Jesus Christ, calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness and new life.
Solomon's story reminds us how far a heart can wander.
The Gospel reminds us where our only lasting hope is found.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth of all is this:
Solomon had a thousand women connected to his throne, but the one thing he could not afford to lose was his wholehearted devotion to God.
May we never gain everything our hearts desire only to discover that we have neglected the One our souls need most.
